blocks.text: About 40 minutes, three parts, 42 questions. Part A gives 24 marks, Part B 6 and Part C 12.
Grade B (350) typically needs at least 30 of 42 marks. The exact boundary varies slightly from test to test.
You hear each recording once only. On paper you get two minutes at the end to check your answers; on computer there is a short pause after each question.
Part A — consultation notes

Two consultations between a health professional and a patient, 4–5 minutes each, with 12 gaps each. You complete the professional's notes as you listen, and you get 30 seconds to read the notes first.
Write the words you hear. Do not paraphrase, repeat words already in the notes, or add information that is not in the recording.
Spelling matters, especially for common medical words such as diabetes or cholesterol. UK and US spellings are both accepted.
In the 30 seconds, predict what fits each gap: a number, a symptom, a drug, a time, a place.
The gaps follow the order of the conversation. If you miss one, leave it and catch the next.
Part B — workplace extracts
Six short extracts from healthcare workplaces, about 45 seconds each, each with one three-option multiple-choice question. You get 15 seconds to read the question first.
Read the question for who is speaking and what the extract is for. The question usually tests the main point, not a single detail.
Part C — presentations and interviews
Two recordings of 4–5 minutes (presentations, interviews or one of each), each with six three-option multiple-choice questions. You get 90 seconds to read the questions.
Listen for opinion and attitude. Wrong options often repeat words you hear but change the meaning.
Questions follow the order of the recording: when the speaker moves on, move on too.
60 minutes, three parts, 42 questions. Part A gives 20 marks, Part B 6 and Part C 16.
Grade B (350) typically needs at least 30 of 42 marks. The exact boundary varies slightly from test to test.
Part A — expeditious reading (15 minutes)

Four short texts on one healthcare topic, such as dosage tables, guidelines or flowcharts, with 20 questions: matching, short answer and sentence completion. Part A is collected after exactly 15 minutes.
Use exactly the word or short phrase from the texts. A misspelt answer gets no mark; UK and US spellings are both accepted.
Abbreviations are not accepted unless they appear in the texts.
First look at titles and layout, so you know which text holds which kind of information.
Don't read every word: scan for key words from the question, then read that sentence carefully.
Part B — short workplace texts
Six short extracts of about 100–140 words, such as policies, emails or guidelines, each with one three-option multiple-choice question. They test the main idea, the purpose and important details.
Ask what the text is for: to inform, to instruct, to warn? The answer is often about purpose.
Part C — longer texts
Two texts of about 800 words, similar to journal or review articles, each with eight four-option multiple-choice questions in the order of the text. Parts B and C together take 45 minutes.
Watch for the writer's opinion and for what is implied, not only what is stated.
If a question asks what a word or phrase refers to, read the sentences just before it.
You get 5 minutes to read the case notes without writing, then 40 minutes to write. You can look at the notes the whole time.
Aim for 180–200 words. There is no automatic penalty outside that range, but a much longer or shorter letter usually loses marks on other criteria.
No particular layout is required, but it must be clear. Use the title and address given in the task.
Abbreviations: some are fine for a colleague in the same field; for a GP or another specialty, write more in full and explain.
A typical referral letter

items: Recipient's name, title and address, then the date.
Re: the patient's name and date of birth.
Purpose: who the patient is and what you are asking for, in the first two lines.
Relevant history and findings, most important first.
Treatment so far and the current situation.
The request in detail: what you want the reader to do, and how urgently.
A closing line, then "Yours sincerely", your name and your role.

blocks.text: Select, don't copy. Include only what this reader needs to continue care.
Turn note form into full sentences, and group related facts instead of following the notes line by line.
Use "Yours sincerely" after "Dear Dr Smith", and "Yours faithfully" after "Dear Sir or Madam".
About 20 minutes in total, with two profession-specific role-plays of about 5 minutes each.
You can make notes on the role-play card and look at it during the role-play. You hand it back at the end.
There is no penalty for not covering every point on the card, but covering more gives more evidence of your English.
Role-plays may include tension: an anxious or angry patient, a misunderstanding, or little time to explain.
Two assessors mark the recording on four linguistic criteria and five areas of clinical communication. Grade B needs mostly 5 of 6 on the linguistic criteria and 2 of 3 on clinical communication.
Use the preparation time to decide which points need a longer explanation and where to ask questions.
A simple shape for each role-play

items: Greet, introduce yourself, and confirm who you are talking to and why.
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Explain in small chunks, in plain language, and check understanding.
